fieldDescription: When and how fast the Threat spreads. The war begins only after the vanilla abyss story flags fire (finding the Onslaught Mk.I or encountering the Threat).
Master switch. Turning this off freezes the war entirely (existing colonies remain).
The swarm was always coming: skip all triggers and begin the war immediately in a new game (takes effect on existing saves too). The story triggers below are ignored while this is on.

Alternate start trigger: a player colony reaching the size below wakes the swarm even without touching the abyss questline - whichever comes first. A maxed colony is exactly the concentration of technology the Threat exists to destroy.
Player colony size that wakes the swarm (6 = vanilla max via natural growth).
How often the war clock advances. Higher = slower everything.

The war begins from one resource-complete OG home system (its full mining/refining/forge chain is founded at once from the Abyss). Values above 1 add that many extra single-colony fringe footholds beyond the OG.
Days a seeded system incubates before a Seeding Swarm is dispatched to found a fabrication colony there.
Hard cap on simultaneously infested systems.
Minimum colony size before it can dispatch colonization waves.

The swarm founds real colonies that grow from size 1 and run a genuinely self-contained hive economy: their mining worlds feed refineries feed forge worlds that build the ships. Shortages of metals or machinery stall growth; hull shortages shrink garrisons and strikes. Cut supply lines and destroy link colonies to starve the network.

Days per size level, multiplied by current size (a size-5 colony takes 300 days to reach 6). Growth is paced by colony health: shortages slow it sharply, and a colony in outright decline loses population instead.
Size cap for Threat colonies.

Spare copies of each production link (refinery, forge, fuel plant) the hive builds as it spreads - one per infested system it holds, up to this many. Under vanilla's economy one producer feeds every hive world that can reach it, so spares add nothing until the original is lost; they exist so that cutting the hive's supply of anything means cutting several worlds. 1 = a single point of failure for each.
Escort strength of colonization fleets: 0 = none, 1 = light, 2 = medium, 3 = heavy.

Days between replacement Defense Swarms fabricating at a colony. This is the hive's whole military tempo: expeditions are mustered FROM the garrison, so this paces strikes and colonization waves too. Killing swarms delays everything until the nexus regrows them - one fleet at a time.

Military options menu at a hive. A colony's garrison, reinforcements bound for it and its Defend Swarms count as defenders wherever they are in the system: while any is alive, raids, bombardment and ground landings wait until it is dealt with. This radius is how far from the world one can be engaged from orbit (Engage waits while they are further out), and any other swarm fleet inside it counts as a defender too. Garrisons orbit 400-700 su out.

Colonies cover each other: a worn-down colony's garrison is topped up by Defense Swarms sent from the best-covered colony that can reach it - same system first, then any system within the donor's fuel range - until garrisons balance out. The swarms physically fly there and can be intercepted en route. A donor must be able to regrow what it sends (Fabrication Core and Swarm Nexus both up) and always keeps one swarm home. To strip a colony bare you must outpace every colony that can reach it, or cut the fuel range that connects them.
How many Defense Swarms the hive may dispatch as reinforcements per colony poll (about half a day). Higher means help arrives in bigger, faster bursts; 1 is a slow trickle.

A garrison slot is a promise of a certain weight of defense. A Defense Swarm shot below this fraction of the fleet points it was fabricated with - or one of a lower tier than the slot wants, such as a small colony's swarm sent to reinforce a big one - is a weak holder: it keeps fighting, but no longer blocks the Swarm Nexus, which grows a proper replacement at its normal respawn cadence and recycles the weak swarm. Lower = damaged swarms hold their slot longer; higher = the hive replaces battle damage sooner.

If on, colony growth is paced by economic health: shortages of core production inputs (ore, metals, volatiles, rare ore/metals) slow and then stop growth until the hive economy recovers. Structure disruption and severe shortages can push a colony into outright decline regardless of this setting.

The first hive system carries Domain-era items, as a swarm out of the Abyss would: a Pristine Nanoforge on its largest forge, and a Mantle Bore, Plasma Dynamo, Catalytic Core or Synchrotron wherever its own deposits leave a production link short. Vanilla's chain only balances at size 8 with these - a plain forge makes 6 hulls against a Swarm Nexus wanting 8, a Pristine one makes 9. Every later colony draws on the home hive, so the items lift the whole swarm, and they are the loot for taking it. Applies to existing saves on the next tick.

Chance that any forge outside the home system's Pristine one carries a Corrupted Nanoforge (plus 1 hull, plus 20 percent quality). A fixed roll per world, so the answer never changes from month to month and a rebuilt forge keeps its luck. 0 disables.

The hive is a closed economy that never trades with the Core worlds, so vanilla's distance-from-Core accessibility penalty models a supply line it doesn't have. This cancels that penalty for hive colonies: 1 removes it fully, 0 leaves vanilla behavior (fringe seeds far from the Core then import almost nothing and stall). Distance from the rest of the hive does not move accessibility either way - vanilla's same-faction proximity term is only ever a bonus.

Shipping units (in and out) a hive world keeps while its Megaport or Spaceport is disrupted. Vanilla keeps a disrupted port counted as present and same-faction shipping never falls below 5 units, so on its own a disrupted hive port changes nothing. At the default 3 a mature world's factories run on a trickle - a size-8 forge gets 3 of the 8 metals it wants - growth stalls, fuel reach shrinks, and its own output reaches the rest of the hive only as that trickle. Kept above zero on purpose: with the Fabrication Core also down, machinery is imported, and zero shipping made a port cut deadlier than a Core cut. 0 = nothing docks at all; -1 = leave vanilla behavior.
If on, worlds decivilized by Threat bombardment become colonization targets - the swarm moves into the graveyards it creates, even inside inhabited systems.

From phase 3, the colonial defense boards offer missions against specific hive infrastructure (rare mining, fuel, refining, swarm nexus) - ordinary contracts that arrive over the comm network and must be accepted before they expire, each explaining what cutting that link does to the swarm. Several offers stand at once, ranked by network impact against difficulty, and the weakest is withdrawn when a more valuable target comes online. Accept one and the completion clock starts. Disruption pays half, decivilization pays full; failing or abandoning costs reputation with the sponsoring faction.
Payout per target colony size (a size-6 hive world pays 6x this for destruction, half for disruption).
How long an offer stays posted before it is withdrawn unaccepted. Real days - deliberately NOT compressed by the debug fast clock.

Days you have to complete a contract once you accept it. Real days - deliberately NOT compressed by the debug fast clock, since this is your window to act. Missing the deadline is a mission failure and costs reputation with the sponsor.

How many contracts the defense boards keep offered at once. Accepted contracts do not count - take all three and the board refills. Offers on a lever already open are discounted when picking the next, so the list spreads across rare mining, fuel, refining and nexus rather than stacking on one.

How much better a new objective must score than the weakest offered one before it displaces it - 1.35 means it must score a third higher again. Lower values make the board churn more aggressively; 1.0 means any improvement triggers a swap. Accepted contracts are never displaced. Note LunaLib renders these descriptions through a text formatter, so avoid literal percent signs here.
Days a newly posted offer is guaranteed before it can be withdrawn for a better one - your window to decide. Offers are also never withdrawn while you are in the target's system.

How far a target's score is raised for sitting inside a faction navy's operating radius (a Patrol HQ, Military Base or High Command within Response Range). A hive world that has crept into defended space is the sector's immediate problem, and is cheaper to kill besides - task forces grind its garrison and a purge expedition may finish it, which still completes your contract in full. 0 ignores faction proximity entirely.

Reward premium on the strategic (expensive) tier over the immediate (cheap) tier. The strategic board names the decisive target regardless of what taking it costs, so it pays more for the same colony size.

Phases are capability, not calendar. Phase 1: fringe expansion (no attacks). Phase 2: begins when some colony can actually stage a strike (strike-sized, forged, fueled). Phase 3: core worlds in reach once some colony can field a full-budget armada (size 6+ with a near-nominal hull economy). Burn forges, cut fuel, or shrink colonies and the phase genuinely regresses.
If on, phase 3 eventually puts the core worlds (size 6+ colonies) in reach.
Large Threat colonies launch strike fleets at inhabited worlds - real fleets you can intercept and fight alongside the defenders. Worlds they decivilize may be converted into new hive colonies.
Sector-wide cap on simultaneous Threat strikes. 0 = unlimited: every hive system with the means keeps a strike in flight.

Light-years of reach per unit of fuel an expedition carries - one rule for everyone. Reach = this x the smaller of fuel available at the launching colony and the fuel its fleets can carry (the tier settings below times vanilla's fleet-size figure for the colony). Hive strikes and seeding waves range from their staging colony by it; faction task forces and siege expeditions, and your own commissioned expeditions, range from their military world by it. A colony with no fuel sends nothing.

Fuel units an expedition carries at a fleet-size figure of 100 percent. Faction and player worlds use vanilla's own fleet-size figure untouched - colony size, doctrine, hull shortage, stability, alpha core, skills, the Fleets percentage on the colony screen - so a 300 percent world carries 12 and is bound by fuel instead. Hive worlds use hive vitality x size / 4: a healthy size-4 hive lifts a full load (20 light-years at the defaults), size 8 twice that, a size-2 foothold half, and a besieged world less as its vitality falls. All the fuel in the sector is no use to a colony that only fields small fleets.
Minimum colony size before it launches strikes (replaces the old 'saturated' stage).

Scales how heavily each mustered Defense Swarm is re-embodied as an expedition fleet. Strikes are drawn from the colony's REAL garrison (everything above its defensive reserve, only at full strength), so their size is fundamentally set by the garrison the colony fields - this multiplier just up- or down-tiers the fleets.
Minimum days between strikes that target YOUR colonies specifically. NPC worlds get no such mercy.

If on, a strike still PREPARING at its staging colony is stillborn when that colony's forge is broken: raid the forge into disruption, bombard the colony, or destroy it before the fleets depart. Once an expedition departs it is autonomous and cannot be recalled.

If on, Threat strikes may target story-critical worlds and decivilize them outright (the engine normally refuses the killing blow). WARNING: erasing quest worlds can permanently break unfinished vanilla storylines. If off, strikes never target story-critical worlds at all.

OFF by default. If on, Threat strikes go back to saturation bombardment: one pass per world that wounds it, or erases a world already ground to the destroy threshold. With it off, strikes soften a world's defenses with tactical bombardment and then LAND a Threat ground front - only a ground victory destroys a colony, for the swarm exactly as for you.

If on, a Threat strike lands a persistent Threat-owned ground front on an inhabited world once its tactical-bombardment structures are suppressed, and that front pushes the colony's strata until it takes them all (the colony is lost) or is beaten. Off, strikes only bombard tactically and never land.

Passes a Threat expedition may deliver against each world in its target system: one softens the defenses, one lands the world's share of the troop pool, and any further pass tops up what is left of that share (a landing turned back by a held orbit gets another try).

The troop pool a Threat strike carries, per difficulty point of the swarms it musters (each swarm is 3 to 9 points): fixed at launch, discounted by losses on the way, split evenly across the worlds in the sweep and shown on the strike's intel. A strike lands what it brought and nothing more - the target's defenses decide the outcome, never the size of the invasion.
A world's share of the troop pool is never below this: a small strike lands fewer worlds rather than token forces (a landing that would fall below the front minimum is called off).
Days of heavy-armaments supply a Threat landing carries. A Threat front is never resupplied except by a further pass of the same expedition - hold out past its supply and it withers.

How much of a colony's banked war-reserve marines count toward its ground defense when an enemy front is on the surface. 1.0 = every banked marine defends; 0 = the reserve is warehouse stock only and does not fight.

How much more often a colony with a Patrol HQ, Military Base, High Command or Lion's Guard counter-attacks a front on its surface. Colony counter-attack cadence is otherwise paced by stability instead of hive vitality.

Disruption days at which a human colony's defense structure (Ground Defenses, Heavy Batteries, Patrol HQ, Military Base, High Command) contributes nothing. Its bonus scales down in a straight line to that point instead of vanilla's on/off, and recovers the same way.

Fraction of a suppressed structure's bonus that bombardment from orbit cannot take away, on a hive's war-strata and a colony's defense structures alike. Once a front stands on the world the floor is 0: boots finish what orbit started.

Disruption days an unopposed besieging fleet (a Threat strike, a siege expedition, a Support sortie, the player's own tactical bombardment) adds per day to a colony's defense structures at overwhelming strength; scaled by fleet / (fleet + defense).

The same over a hive's war-strata, whose clock is Disruption Wear Days rather than Fortification Disruption Days. Higher because a hive's defense figure is anchored to its size and runs several times a colony's: at the default a 600-point expedition takes a size-5 hive to the floor in about 60 days. Both rates are net of the clock's own run-down.
A besieging fleet's points are multiplied by this before being weighed against the world's ground-defense figure, for both suppression and return fire.

Fraction of a besieging fleet's points the world's Ground Defenses and Heavy Batteries destroy per day at even odds, scaled by the batteries' share of the defense and their condition. Ships are lost smallest first; the flagship is spared.
Days of siege one tactical bombardment by the player stands for: it suppresses and takes return fire as a besieging fleet would over that many days.
Whether a planetary shield absorbs part of the disruption a bombardment would land on everything else on the world. Off, the shield is an ordinary structure.

Fraction of incoming disruption a fully intact planetary shield turns aside. It falls in a straight line as the shield's own disruption days pile up, on the same clock as the world's defense structures, so each bombardment buys less cover for the next. The orbital floor applies to the shield as well: orbit alone can never quite spend one, but a front on the ground removes the floor.

Disruption a planetary shield takes itself from a bombardment, as a multiple of what one of the world's defense structures takes from the same pass. The shield has no cover of its own. Above 1 it burns out faster than the guns it protects; below 1 it outlasts them.

What a planetary shield adds to the colony's ground defense at full condition. Vanilla gives a flat 2 (a x3 multiplier) and strips all of it the moment the shield is disrupted; this mod gives the shield a different job - absorbing bombardment - so the default is 0. Set to 2 for vanilla's figure, applied in proportion to the shield's condition rather than as an on/off switch.
Days a strike or siege expedition holds orbit over each target world before giving the siege up and moving on.
A world whose Threat front has run dry weighs this much more as the next strike's target: the front signals, the next expedition answers and resupplies it.
Days a dry Threat front digs in waiting for the next expedition before it spends itself in a final push. The swarm does not extract.
Stability a colony loses per district an invader holds.
Accessibility a colony loses per district an invader holds.
Disruption days a seized civilian industry is pinned at while the invader holds its district; it recovers that fast once the district is retaken.
A Threat ground victory over a human colony seeds a hive on the world at once. Off: the world decivilises and the swarm comes back for the ruins later.
Size of the hive seeded on a conquered world.

Overall scale on hive ground-defense strength. This is the input to raid effectiveness AND the base of the bombardment fuel bill, so it scales both how costly marines are and how costly fuel is. Hive defenses keep firing at half effect while disrupted, so repeat passes are never near-free.

Every hive lives deep underground behind ground defenses anchored to colony size (400 points per size by default, immune to unrest, multiplied by the defense industries - a mature hive's true figure runs into the thousands). Bombardment can NEVER reduce a hive's population: saturation costs the full defense figure for days of disruption, tactical costs a fraction and suppresses the war-strata longer, marines cut deepest. The only way a hive dies is decline - its population falling to size 1 under sustained disruption or shortages.

Flat ground-defense points per colony size, before industry multipliers (a size-4 hive fields a 1600-point base, size-8 fields 3200; ground defenses, heavy batteries and the nexus multiply it further). This is the number bombardment fuel costs are priced from, and it drives marine raid effectiveness and casualties. Hive defenses ignore unrest - the machines do not riot.
Defense multiplier bonus from the hive Ground Defenses structure: mult = 1 + bonus (x2 at the default 1.0). Scaled down by machinery/metals shortages.
Defense multiplier bonus from hive Heavy Batteries: mult = 1 + bonus (x3 at the default 2.0). Scaled down by machinery/metals shortages.
Defense multiplier bonus from the Swarm Nexus: mult = 1 + bonus (x1.5 at the default 0.5).

Disruption days on a hive structure's clock at which it has worn to nothing: a defense structure's bonus, and a disrupted Core's fabrication factor, both fall in a straight line to zero at this many days - the hive's fortification clock. From orbit alone a war-stratum never falls below the Fortification Orbital Floor; a front on the ground takes it the rest of the way. Marine raids add their days, and a ground front that holds adds a net day per day, so an organ carrying 300 days has had an army on top of it for most of a year. The size-anchored base defense never wears, so bombardment gets cheaper as a siege grinds on but never free. 0 disables wear.
Scale on the saturation fuel bill. At 1.0 saturation costs exactly the colony's ground-defense strength.
Tactical bombardment fuel cost as a fraction of the colony's ground-defense strength - concentrated fire on exposed military targets is far cheaper than saturating the world.
Days of disruption a saturation pass inflicts on a hive's industries (vanilla is 365 - the hive's deep strata reknit almost immediately).

Days of disruption a tactical bombardment marked by your own ground front writes to the hive's Fabrication Core and port (the front loses marines to the barrage). The bombardment's effect on the war-strata is the siege slice, not this.
Multiplier on marine casualties when raiding hive worlds - the counter-swarms contest every corridor.

A persistent army: land marines and heavy armaments on a hive world (Ground operations, on the military options menu) and they stay, fighting after you break orbit. The front burns heavy armaments as upkeep - the stockpile is its supply countdown - and marines attrit at flat daily rates, faster once the armaments run dry. Strong enough (against the world's current, worn defense figure) it HOLDS - suppressing the hive's organs and able to push the stratum campaign below; weaker it GRINDS only the outer defenses until they wear down; weaker still it is a mere foothold. Resupply and withdraw by docking; live Defense Swarms in orbit block that, so the hive's reinforcement network is the counter-siege.
Master switch for the ground-front mechanic. Existing fronts keep ticking if turned off mid-siege; the deploy option is hidden.

Effective strength (troops x entrenchment) as a fraction of the colony's current ground-defense figure needed to HOLD - suppress every key structure and be able to push. Below it the front only grinds or survives. 0.17 keeps the old landing sizes viable now that a dug-in front fights at 1.0 rather than 1.5.

Fraction of the defense figure needed to GRIND: too weak to reach the deep organs, the front harasses the Ground Defenses and Heavy Batteries at the reduced rate below. As they wear, the hold requirement falls and the front upgrades itself - the path from an early landing to a full siege.

Days added to each suppressed structure's disruption clock per day held. The clock counts down one day per day naturally, so 2.0 nets +1 day of accumulated wear per day - and the clock is the same wear mechanic raids and bombardments feed (see Disruption Wear Days).
Suppression-rate multiplier while only grinding the defense structures.
Fraction of the front's current marines lost per 30 days while supplied - the hive contests the ground forever, so a siege is never free.
Attrition multiplier once the front's heavy armaments run out.

Heavy armaments the front consumes per marine per 30 days. At the default a landing carries 1 armament per marine for its supply days and burns them faster the bigger it is. What the front has on hand is exactly how long it lasts unsupplied - legible and plannable.
Days of digging in to reach the full entrenchment multiplier below. Rewards sustained sieges over drive-by landings.
Effectiveness multiplier of a fully dug-in front. A landing starts at the landing multiplier below and ramps to this over the entrenchment days; the ramp is frozen while pushing.
Effectiveness multiplier of a fresh landing before it has dug in. Attackers land exposed; the defenders' entrenchment is their ground-defense figure.
Fraction of its entrenchment a front keeps when it takes a stratum or district, or is battered by a counter-attack. Pushing costs cover; holding earns it.
Marines below which the front is overrun outright.

If on, a tactical bombardment with your own front deployed costs it marines (fraction below) - and in exchange the ground forces mark targets, so the strike's disruption also lands on the Fabrication Core and port, not just the war-strata.
Fraction of the front's marines lost to each danger-close tactical pass.

Fraction of an enemy ground front the swarm kills per 30 days while it holds the orbit over its own hive unopposed, scaled by its weight against what the front can put in the way. This replaced the scour, which annihilated a front outright once the swarm had held the orbit for a few days - a guillotine on a timer that predated the siege system and cut across all of it. Contest the orbit and the bombardment stops. 0 disables.

Minimum total Threat fleet points at the planet for the swarm to count as holding the orbit. A bombardment is a fleet operation - a lone battered frigate (~5-15 FP) cannot mount one, but the smallest real Defense Swarm (~83 FP) can. Raise toward 150-300 to demand a serious battle group.

Days after a saturation bombardment during which ground forces cannot land - the surface is a radiological ruin. Keep this at or above the saturation disruption duration, or sat bombing becomes the best siege opener instead of a tradeoff (its role is silencing a world, at the price of ground tempo).

How far below a threshold a front must fall before it gives up the state it holds. The defence figure now moves every tick because the garrison bleeds, so without a band a front sitting on the line would flap between holding and grinding and announce every flip.

A colony defends with the marines in its resource stockpile - never with personal Storage, which stays yours alone. Those marines are called up over days rather than instantly, they take casualties when a front presses them, and they gain experience the way vanilla marines do: a hard fight teaches, a curbstomp teaches nothing. Level is experience over headcount and the rank is vanilla own - Regular, Experienced, Veteran, Elite - so a front reads the same as the marines in your hold. Hives have none of this: their strength is structural and erodes by losing strata instead.

Weight the colony stockpiled marines enter a COUNTER-ATTACK at; they defend at full weight regardless. Holding a line and mounting an offensive are different jobs. At 1.0 a big stockpile becomes a sledgehammer that overruns any beachhead outright, which is exactly what this knob exists to stop.

How much the force ratio speeds up or slows a colony counter-attack cadence. Before 0.6.6 the cadence read stability alone, so a colony with 5,000 marines went over the top exactly as often as one with 50. At 3.0 a world that outmatches the beachhead threefold hits three times as often, and one being overrun three-to-one manages a third as many. Set to 1 to go back to stability alone. Note this pairs with Defender Counter-Attack Losses: more tempo means more attempts, and every attempt costs marines.

Days a colony takes to call up, arm and post its whole marine stockpile. Marines shipped in mid-siege ramp in over this instead of defending the same afternoon; marines that leave stop defending at once. Set very low for the old instant behaviour.

Fraction of a colony armed marines lost each time it counter-attacks, win or lose - bouncing off a dug-in front is the expensive case. At 0 the defenders counter-attack for free, as they did before 0.6.6.

Fraction of a colony armed marines lost per 30 days while a front presses it at full strength, scaled down by what the front can actually bring to bear. This is what turns the garrison from a fixed wall into something a siege can grind down by fighting.
Strength bonus of a fully elite pool. Vanilla own figure for elite marines is 1.0, meaning +100 percent.
Casualty reduction of a fully elite pool. Vanilla own figure is 0.5, meaning half losses.

Experience multiplier per ground action, on vanilla own raid figure. Experience gained is one minus that side effectiveness, times its headcount, times this - so the side that was outmatched learns the most and an easy win teaches nobody anything.
Veterancy level an NPC or Threat landing musters at, from 0 for raw troops to 1 for elite. The player landings inherit the fleet own marine rank instead of this.

If on, a landing inherits your fleet marine rank, writes back what it earned when it withdraws, and your Planetary Operations and Tactical Drills skills apply to your ground fronts. Turn off to keep this veterancy entirely separate from vanilla.

A size-S hive is S strata deep with the Fabrication Core at the center - and ERADICATION IS A GROUND VICTORY, the only way a hive dies. A front strong enough to hold can be ordered to push: each stratum taken strips its share of the base defenses and of the hive's output, and taking the last one destroys the Core and the colony. After each stratum the front consolidates at a checkpoint, requests reinforcement, and - given no orders within the window - pushes on by doctrine; you can instead order it to entrench and stand fast, or pull it out (which requires controlling the space over the planet). The hive counter-attacks on a cadence paced by its health: starving its economy is what makes those counter-attacks rare and feeble. NPC expeditions land their own fronts and run the same campaign.

A front strong enough to hold assaults the next stratum as soon as its troops are on the ground, and again when troop reinforcements bring it back to holding strength. A Dig in order holds until the next troops land. Off, your fronts push only when ordered; NPC and Threat fronts run their own doctrine either way.

A front that holds NO ground is destroyed outright by a counter-attack rather than pushed back, and assaulting costs it all of its cover - so if an assault would get it overrun, it breaks off and digs in first, resuming once entrenchment or the odds make one survivable. Its own fleet will not bombard over troops in the open either: the troops take cover first, and the guns speak only if that was not enough. Fronts that already hold ground do not dig in - for them a counter-attack takes a district back, which is a setback rather than a death.

Base days one stratum push takes at even strength; scaled by the defense-to-strength ratio (clamped 0.5x to 3x), so an overwhelming front advances in days and a marginal one crawls. As strata fall and strip base defense, later pushes genuinely get faster.
Fraction of the front's marines lost per 30 days while assaulting (replaces the entrenched attrition rate for the duration). Pushing is how you win and how you bleed.
Heavy-armaments burn multiplier while assaulting - offensives eat materiel.
Effectiveness multiplier of a front whose heavy armaments have run out - marines without materiel fight at this fraction of their strength, on top of the raised attrition. Resupply before pushing.

Off (default): the swarm's ground fronts do not fight on heavy armaments at all - they burn none, never run dry, and take none of the dry penalties, because nothing in the game can ever resupply them. On: the old rule, where a Threat landing lives off what it brought, digs in when it runs out and spends itself in a final push.

Casualty multiplier on a Threat ground front while it is assaulting, on top of the ordinary push rate. This is what the swarm pays instead of starving, now that it can break up its own ships for replacements. It does not apply while they are dug in - make them come to you.
Defense multiplier of a dug-in (non-pushing) front against hive counter-attacks. A front caught mid-assault defends without it.
Days a front consolidates after taking a stratum, requesting reinforcement and awaiting orders. Told nothing, it pushes on by doctrine; order it to entrench to stop the advance.

Base days between hive counter-attacks against a front, DIVIDED by the colony's health - a starved colony at 25 percent health attacks four times more rarely. A counter-attack that beats the front's (entrenchment-boosted) strength retakes a held stratum and costs marines; one that doubles a stratum-less beachhead destroys it.
Fraction of the front's marines lost to a counter-attack it fails to repel.
Days of heavy-armaments supply an NPC expedition's ground landing carries. When it runs dry the front withers; the next expedition lands a fresh one.

NPC factions behave exactly as vanilla until the Threat strikes one of their colonies - that strike puts the faction in WAR MODE. A mobilised faction's colonies accrue visible reserves of marines, heavy armaments, fuel and supplies, each banked from the colony's vanilla surplus of the matching commodity (a War Footing condition adds the war's demand, and the depot covers the colony's own shortage first), and every expedition draws its landing force and provisions from the colony it sails from - troops that ride the fleets as real cargo. Colonies ship stock to those staging bases by convoy: real fleets, interceptable, lootable. Your own faction mobilises the same way when the swarm first strikes a world of yours.
Master switch for war mode, per-colony reserves, convoys and fleet orders. Off, expeditions raise abstract troops as before.
Days after its last strike a mobilised faction stands down - only if no live hive remains in expedition range of its military worlds. Reserves are kept, frozen. 0 = mobilised for good.

Comma-separated faction ids that never mobilise. The Threat still strikes their worlds and they stay hostile to it, but they raise no task forces, sieges, convoys or ground fronts and keep no war reserve - raiders, not a navy. A faction already mobilised on a save stands down on the next poll, reserves kept.

NPC colonies only. Each 30 days a mobilised NPC colony banks its vanilla SURPLUS of each reserve commodity - availability above demand, in econ units - times the commodity's econ unit (1,500 fuel, 750 supplies, 200 heavy armaments, 100 marines) times this. A colony in deficit banks nothing; selling to a colony raises its availability and so its banking for the sale's duration. Your own colonies' reserve is their resource stockpile, which vanilla fills at its own rate (a Waystation raises it); this knob does not touch it.

Every colony of a mobilised faction carries the War Footing condition, which adds vanilla demand for marines, heavy armaments, fuel and supplies: this many units at size 5, scaled by size / 5 and rounded up (1.0: sizes 3-5 add 1 unit, 6-8 add 2). A colony that was only just balanced now shows a shortage - the war eating its margin. 0 adds no demand.

The depot counters the colony's own shortage first: while a mobilised colony is short of a reserve commodity, its reserve issues the quantity that lifts availability by the deficit - a trade modifier, the way a sale would be - and issues again when it lapses. Never more than this fraction of the stock at hand per issue, and only whole units; when the stock cannot buy one unit the shortage stands and the war board says so.
Days one issue from the depot holds a colony's availability up before the reserve pays again. 0 turns shortage covering off.
A colony stockpiles at most this many months of its own production of each commodity.
Months of its own production each colony holds the moment its faction mobilises - the peacetime depots the first sortie draws from. 0 starts every reserve empty.
NPC expeditions and sorties never draw a colony below this fraction of its cap - the home garrison's stock. Keeps a small faction from emptying its depots on one sortie and going quiet.
Your own orders never draw one of your colonies below this fraction of its cap. 0 lets a siege or convoy commit the whole stock - stockpiled marines also count toward the colony's ground defence.
Marines every colony raises per size per 30 days regardless of industry, so no colony sits permanently at zero. For your own colonies they land in the resource stockpile.

A colony is a base - stages, sails sorties and convoys, sends and receives them - only with a military structure AND a functional Waystation, vanilla's stockpiling structure. A hive world needs its Swarm Nexus, as its strikes already do. Disrupting either by raid severs the base. Off: a military structure alone is enough, as before.

An NPC faction entering war mode builds a Waystation at each of its military worlds with a spaceport (only one vanilla market ships with one). You build your own. Off: NPC factions field only the bases they already have.

Exponent on every ground-war strength ratio - push pace, push attrition, counter-attack losses and overruns. 1 is linear and legible; 2 is Lanchester's square law, where concentrating twice the marines pays four times over. Dialog quotes stay exact at any value.
An expedition waits - and its base keeps calling convoys - unless the base holds this fraction of the marines the landing needs. 0 sails with whatever is there.

The board's "Extra" siege button commits this multiple of the marines the assault needs (the "Siege" button); "All" commits the whole reserve above its floor. The flotilla grows to carry the bigger landing and is trimmed to the base's free fleet points.
Fuel an expedition or task force draws from its base per fleet point per light-year of distance. A cost, not a gate.
Supplies an expedition or task force draws from its base per fleet point. A cost, not a gate.
Troop-transport share of a cargo-carrying expedition fleet (vanilla composition multiplier). Too low and the marines drawn will not all fit - the remainder stays home.
Whether mobilised factions ship reserves between their colonies by convoy. Off, each staging base fights with what it makes itself.
Light-years a donor colony will ship to a staging base.
Marines one convoy carries at most (transports are sized to the load). Fewer, larger convoys lose a smaller share per attack - keep this high.
Units of armaments, fuel and supplies one convoy carries at most.

The board's "Med" load button asks for this multiple of what a front or colony is short of; "Max" asks for a full hull load of everything the source can spare. Every tier is still capped by the source's spare stock and the convoy's capacity.
Combat fleet points every convoy sails with, before the cargo-value escort below.
Extra escort fleet points per 1,000 of cargo value (marines count 1 each, armaments 0.5, fuel and supplies 0.1). A rich convoy is a real fleet.
A base's shortfall, as a fraction of one convoy load, below which no convoy sails.
Convoys one faction dispatches per 30-day tick at most, its neediest bases first. Fewer, larger convoys are safer than many small ones.

Mobilised factions run supply convoys to their ground fronts (marines and heavy armaments from the nearest base's reserve) and withdrawal convoys for fronts that call for a pickup. Runs wait at the hive system's jump-point while Defense Swarms hold the orbit - a garrisoned hive strangles the front.
Days of heavy-armaments upkeep a supply run tops a front up to.
A supply run reinforces a front back toward this fraction of its peak marine strength.
Days a supply or withdrawal run waits at the jump-point for the orbit to clear before turning for home with its cargo.
Hive colonies near a convoy's route may detach one Defense Swarm to hunt it - the swarm's own commerce raiding, paid for with a thinner garrison while it is out.
Light-years from a convoy route's midpoint within which a hive colony may send a raider.
Chance each eligible hive colony (Defense Swarms above its reserve) detaches a raider at a passing convoy; the nearest rolls first and one raider is enough.
Days a raider hunts its convoy before turning for home.
Fraction of its own cap a donor colony keeps back for itself.
A staging base stocks this many expeditions' worth of each reserve.
Days after which a convoy that has not arrived is written off with its cargo.

The war board's faction view lets you command your own mobilised navy from anywhere: guard a colony's orbit, stage materiel to it by convoy, hold a hive system's jump-point, send a siege, recall a fleet - each limited by what the sending colony can field (see Player Aid). Other factions' navies are their own.
Whether the faction view offers Guard, Stage, Intercept, Siege and Recall for your own faction.

Combat fleet points of an NPC faction's guard or intercept task force. Your own task forces sail with everything the colony has free; this is only the free points a colony needs to be picked first as the source.
Days a guard task force holds a colony's orbit before returning to base.

Days a task force guarding one of your own colonies stays before returning; 0 = until recalled. While it is there its points are that colony's to send out, and a siege, intercept, escort or guard from there takes it along - the way to stage fleets at a staging base.
Days an intercept task force holds a hive system's jump-point.

A combat sortie that holds the orbit over a besieged world your faction has a ground front on, clears it of whatever contests it, and besieges it: its fleet points suppress the world's defenses each day like any siege fleet's, and the batteries answer. While the orbit is contested and no friendly warship holds it, supply and evacuation runs to that front are refused outright. Factions fly Support too.
Days a Support task force holds a besieged world's orbit before returning to base.

A combat sortie that holds the orbit over a world and fights whatever contests it, but bombards only while your ground front there cannot hold - it keeps its ships where Support spends them. Factions fly Defend too.
Days a Defend task force holds a world's orbit before returning to base.

An expedition fleet that has landed or reinforced a ground front leaves its expedition and stays over the world on Defend until the front is gone, and a fleet with nothing left to land joins it instead of bombarding a world it cannot take. Off: the expedition sweeps on as before.
A landing's Defend stands down and goes home once the batteries have ground the fleet below this fraction of its strength on arrival.

Once a Defend fleet has bombarded a world's defences to the orbital floor and its ground front still cannot hold, it stops bombarding and breaks up its own ships for troops instead, landing them on the front. It stops as soon as the front holds, and does not go home while it is doing it. Off: the fleet simply holds the orbit.
Troops landed for each fleet point of hulls broken up. Ships go smallest first; the flagship and the last hull are always spared.
How far past the hold line the fabrication aims, so the front does not sit on the boundary and oscillate. 1.05 = five per cent of daylight. The fleet never commits more than this needs.
Days of heavy armaments each batch of fabricated troops brings down with it, at the front's own burn rate. Below a landing's 90 days: they are improvised, not equipped.

Off: a Support or Defend fleet, and a swarm's station, holds the orbit - it fights what attacks it or meets it there and never pursues. On: it chases what it sees and is leashed back from 1,500 units out, which left at most one of four Defend fleets at the planet on any day.

Defenders within 1,500 units of a world - a hive's Defense Swarms, a colony's station and patrols - hold its orbit against a faction only while their fleet points are at least this fraction of that faction's own warships there. With nothing friendly there, any defender holds it. While an orbit is held nothing bombards, passes or lands; the fleets fight for it.

What you send from your own colonies to other factions from the war board: a task force to defend a colony, a convoy of what it is short of, a task force at a hive's door. Sized by what your colony can field, paid in credits, earning standing on arrival. Other factions' navies are their own; they ask for help on the mission board and help each other by standing.
Whether the faction view offers Defend, Aid and Strike to other factions, and the capacity ledger limits what your colonies launch.

Fleet points a colony of yours can have at sea at once, times its vanilla Fleet size percentage (colony size, doctrine, ship-hull shortage, stability). Every fleet launched from it through the board holds points until it is home.
Days a lost fleet's points stay held against its colony.
A colony sends no task force smaller than this.
Relationship (-1 to 1) below which a faction refuses your aid. A faction at war with you always refuses.
Credits of delivered goods, at the receiving market's price, per point of standing (1 point = 0.01 relationship).
Most points one delivery earns.

fieldName: Standing for a Guard on Station
fieldDescription: Points when a task force you sent reaches the colony.

fieldName: Standing for a Guard Term Served
fieldDescription: Points when it serves its full term.

fieldName: Standing for a Task Force at the Door
fieldDescription: Points split among every faction with a colony in the hive's strike reach when your task force holds its jump-point.
Whether mobilised factions post defence and delivery contracts on the mission board.
How many requests stand unaccepted at once.
Days a defence contract runs: it pays if no Threat action lands on the colony in that time and you (or a guard you sent) were there for each strike.
Credits a defence contract pays per size of the colony.
A colony asks for defence when the incoming strike's strength exceeds its defenders' (faction strength in the system plus the station) times this.
Days a vanilla deficit must stand before a colony asks for the commodity; an exhausted depot asks at once.
An aid contract pays the goods' value at the receiving market times this.
Standing for a delivery is multiplied by this when it answers an open request.
Whether mobilised factions guard and resupply each other's colonies by standing - and yours.
Chance per 30-day tick per need that a fully willing (Cooperative) ally sends aid; Friendly 0.75x, Welcoming 0.5x, Favourable 0.25x, less nothing.

The swarm answers who hurts it. Every faction earns grudge for strata taken, hives eradicated and raids or tactical passes landed; the sum is the hive's alarm. Both are shown on the war board and fade monthly. Alarm speeds up Swarm Nexus fabrication - the hive's whole military tempo - grudge points its strikes at that faction's worlds, and a ground victory draws an immediate retaliation strike at the winner. No hidden scaling: the numbers are on the board.
Master switch for grudge, alarm and retaliation.
Grudge points a faction earns for each stratum its ground front takes.
Grudge points for destroying a hive's Fabrication Core.
Grudge points for a successful raid or tactical bombardment pass on a hive world.
Fraction of every grudge that fades per 30 days.
Swarm Nexus fabrication-speed bonus per point of alarm: at 0.04, alarm 10 means garrisons - and therefore strikes and expansion - come 1.4 times as fast.
The most alarm can multiply fabrication speed by.
Strike-target weight bonus per point of a faction's grudge: at 0.2, grudge 10 makes that faction's worlds three times as likely to be struck.
A ground victory draws an immediate strike at the winning faction from the nearest hive that can muster one - a strike it could have launched anyway, aimed now.

A mobilised faction's siege calls its allies: every other mobilised faction with a base in reach may answer with a task force holding the hive's jump-point so the siege lands under cover. Your Rally button on a hive row does the same for every ally that takes your orders, plus a siege from the best-supplied of them.
Whether sieges post calls that allied mobilised factions answer.
Days a call stays open for allies to answer.
Chance per 30-day tick that an eligible ally answers an open call with an Intercept task force.

An outpost is a faction-styled orbital station over an uncolonised world - no market, no economy - that blocks the swarm from seeding it until the station is destroyed. You build one over any uncolonised world from its planet dialog (or over purged worlds from the war board) for credits, with a military colony of yours in reach; a mobilised faction pays supplies and fuel from its nearest base and fortifies purged worlds on its own.
Whether outposts can be built: by you over any uncolonised world (planet dialog) or a purged one (faction view), and by mobilised factions over purged worlds.

Whether taking a hive world by ground assault raises a free outpost over it for the winner - and leaves the front's survivors in it as its stockpile. Off: the world is simply dead ground and the survivors come home.
1 orbital station, 2 battlestation, 3 star fortress - in the faction's own style.
What you pay for an outpost.
Supplies a mobilised faction's base pays for an outpost.
Fuel a mobilised faction's base pays for an outpost.
Chance per 30-day tick that a mobilised faction fortifies an open purged world within reach of a base that can pay.

A recalled fleet (or one whose order ran out) comes home on a tracked leg: everything still aboard - marines, armaments, cargo - goes back into the base's reserve, and this fraction of the fuel and supplies it drew at launch is refunded, scaled by its surviving strength. A fleet lost on the way returns nothing.

A hive colony's health is its input satisfaction times the functionality of its fabrication organs. Since the ground-war rework low health only ever WEAKENS: growth stalls, garrisons rebuild slowly, reach shrinks, and counter-attacks against ground forces come rarely and feebly - but no colony dies without a ground victory.

Fabrication factor the moment the Fabrication Core is disrupted; from there it wears in a straight line with the days on the Core's clock (see Disruption Wear Days) to zero at the wear limit. At 1.0 the clock alone decides: one tactical pass leaves 80 percent, a front holding for 150 days half, 300 days nothing - and the hive's counter-attack interval and growth follow. Below 1.0 a fresh disruption also takes a step.
Colony health at or below which growth stops entirely (without yet declining).
Colony health at or above which the colony grows at its full configured pace; growth ramps linearly between the stall and full-pace thresholds.

When a Threat strike targets an NPC colony, its faction musters a task force against the attacking colony's garrison. Nearby navies also launch siege expeditions - tactical bombardments and commando raids that suppress a hive's organs and push it into decline, including (rarely, with extra escorts) full assaults on defended colonies. Only factions the swarm has struck (war mode) launch them, from a base colony's war reserve; your own are ordered from the war board's faction view the same way.
If on, an NPC faction whose colony is struck sends a counter-task-force against the attacking colony's Defense Swarms (only if it has a military world within range).
Sector-wide cap on simultaneous faction task forces / purge expeditions. 0 = unlimited.
Smallest task force a responding faction sends (fleet difficulty 0-10 scale).
Largest task force a responding faction sends.
Higher = weaker task forces for the same faction military strength. Task force difficulty = min + factionStrength / this.

Siege expeditions, NPC and commissioned alike, are sized to the target's defenses: an industry raid only lands when the ground force is at least a third of the defender strength, so fleets are added until the estimated ground strength clears that with headroom. NPC ground strength is a quarter of crew capacity, which tracks fleet size - one difficulty point of fleet lands about this much (measured: 22 points landed 947). Lower it if raids keep being repulsed, raise it if sieges arrive absurdly large.

Cap on how many fleets a siege expedition grows to while sizing itself to the target's defenses. Sizing assumes the tactical pass has already suppressed the war-strata (about 60 percent of the intact figure): a size-8 hive behind Heavy Batteries then needs about 3,600 ground strength, which is 9 full-size fleets. When the cap still leaves the force short, the commission quote says so and NPC sieges settle for the tactical bombardment.

A siege expedition clears the orbit before it bombards or lands: while Defense Swarms hold the orbit of a target world no siege pass is delivered there, and the expedition's fleets at that world - within Siege Hunt Range - hunt the swarms down. Off, the fleets ignore the swarms (as vanilla raid fleets do) and spend their passes on commando raids whenever the landing is refused - which is how a single swarm ship used to stall a whole siege. Either way the siege leash keeps them on their target.

How far from a contested world an expedition fleet will hunt for its orbit. The fight for the orbit is bounded by the range the contest itself is measured over: a defender that breaks off further than this is no longer holding the orbit, so there is nothing left to fight for and the fleet goes back to its siege.

How far from its nearest target an expedition fleet may stray before it drops what it is doing and returns to the siege. Leaving the target system counts however far away it went. Threat fleets are born to pursue without limit, which once left a strike three weeks and zero passes into chasing one fleet across the sector.

Siege passes an expedition may run against each colony it targets - one tactical bombardment while any war-stratum carries less than 80 percent of a pass, the ground landing once they all do, reinforcement of the front from what is still aboard after that, commando raids where it cannot land. At 2 the first expedition bombs and lands with nothing to spare.

If on, NPC navies launch siege expeditions at Threat colonies: tactical bombardments and commando raids that suppress a hive's organs and push it into decline - they can genuinely wither and erase colonies without your help, though never by bombardment alone.
Minimum days between NPC purge expeditions against any one colony.

Hive colonies up to this size are besieged PREEMPTIVELY - navies in range suppress young footholds before they entrench, fighting through their Defense Swarms. Larger defended colonies can draw a full assault too (extra escorts, longer cooldown - see below). 0 disables preemptive sieges.

Cooldown multiplier for full NPC assaults on DEFENDED entrenched colonies (garrisoned, above the preemptive size). Higher = rarer; these expeditions sail with an extra escort fleet to fight through the Defense Swarms.

A WOUNDED colony (open decline meter, or Core/Nexus/port still disrupted) draws the next expedition on this short cooldown instead of the full purge interval - navies press an advantage, turning single visits into sustained campaigns. The decline meter also does not regrow while any key organ is disrupted.
Systems defended by a live Remnant Nexus resist infestation - the swarm must win a war of machines first. Purging the Remnant yourself clears the Threat's path.
If on, the spread cannot claim a system with a live Remnant Nexus without first destroying it in a machine war.
Per-attempt chance the swarm destroys a defending Remnant Nexus. Failures are retried on later spread attempts.
The Threat is a machine menace at war with all life. These control how that reads on the relations screen and whether the sector treats exterminating the swarm as a war crime.

If on, the Threat is pinned to vengeful with every faction (including you), so it reads as openly hostile rather than 'not currently hostile'. If off, it keeps the vanilla neutral default until fleets are forced hostile ad hoc.
If on, saturation-bombarding a Threat colony carries no reputation penalty with civilized factions - exterminating the swarm is not treated as a war crime. If off, vanilla atrocity penalties apply.
Tools for testing. Effects apply on the next war clock check (about half a day of game time).

Playtesting mode: narrator messages for every swarm event, map markers for ALL infested systems (no discovery needed), per-colony economic vitals in the intel, and a purge button to delete a hive system and watch the network react.
Logs spread/colony/strike/economy events to starsector.log (prefix [ThreatInc]).
Starts the war immediately, skipping the story-flag trigger. Turn off again afterward.
Runs the entire war 10x faster for testing: tick cadence, stage durations, growth, garrison respawns, strike intervals, and phase delays.

Grants the Onslaught Mk.I sensor modifications (10x detection range vs Threat fleets) that a normal playthrough earns from the abyss quest. Note: the war start now grants these automatically, so this is only needed for pre-start scouting.

Fires once when toggled on (turn it back off afterward): starts the war if it has not, founds a connected network of mature hive systems across the sector - a home system with its full production chain plus single-colony footholds, every system within Link LY of another hive system and a quota of them within Core LY of a core world - stands up their garrisons, and mobilises every faction that owns a colony (yours excepted: use the board's Mobilise button). For testing the war balance on a fresh save. Existing hive systems count toward the totals.
Fewest hive systems the instant war stands up.
Most hive systems the instant war stands up.
Fewest of those systems placed within Core LY of a core world (a size 6+ colony).
Most systems placed within Core LY of a core world; exceeded only when nothing else is in reach.
Every founded system lies within this many light-years of another hive system.
A system counts as near the core when a core world (a size 6+ colony) lies within this many light-years. A healthy size-4 hive reaches about 16 LY on default fuel settings.
Size of each colony in the home system's production chain. Size 6 with a stable hull supply is the phase-3 bar that opens core worlds to strikes.
Size of the single colony founded in every other system. Size 4 is the default strike bar.

DANGER: wipes the entire war from this save - every Threat colony reverts to an untouched planet, all Threat fleets despawn, all progress clears. The war then restarts from scratch via the normal start triggers. Fires once when toggled on; turn it back off afterward. In-flight strike fleets already dispatched are not recalled and will fight to the end.
